ta-l1d15q2-d1e3501.summary: Opens the question to whom it belongs to be sent, with a first argument that it belongs to the whole Trinity. Damascene says that in God all things are one except ingenerateness, generation, and procession, and mission is none of these.
claims: Everything in God except the personal properties is common to the three.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3504.summary: Second argument. A divine person's mission is understood by that person's being manifested; Augustine says to be sent is to be known to be from another. The effect in the creature made by mission manifests the whole Trinity as an effect manifests its cause.
claims: Effects of mission manifest the whole Trinity.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3507.summary: Third argument. Gifts appropriated to the Father, such as power, are communicable to creatures just as those appropriated to the Son and Spirit (wisdom, goodness), by reason of which they are said to be sent. So the Father would be sent for the same reason.
claims: Power, appropriated to the Father, is also given to creatures.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3511.summary: Fourth argument. Wherever the Son or Spirit is, the Father is too. They are said to be sent because they exist in a new way in a creature, so the Father is sent with them and mission belongs to the whole Trinity.
claims: Where the Son or Spirit is, the Father is.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3514.summary: Contrary argument that only the Son is sent. To be sent is to be known to be from another (Augustine), and knowledge is appropriated to the Son, the Word and Wisdom of the Father.
claims: Knowledge is appropriated to the Son.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3517.summary: Second contrary argument that only the Spirit is sent. All spiritual gifts pertain to the manifestation of the Spirit (1 Cor. 12:7), and by mission a divine person is manifested.
claims: All spiritual gifts manifest the Spirit.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3523.summary: Thomas's determination. Every mission implies some authority of someone over the one sent. Among divine persons there is authority only by origin, so being sent belongs only to a person who is from another, with respect to whom authority can be found in another. So Son and Spirit are said to be sent, not the Father or the Trinity itself.
claims: Only the persons who are from another, Son and Spirit, can be sent.
Authority among divine persons exists only by origin.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3526.summary: Reply to the first argument. Mission implicitly includes the notion of procession and generation as to what they have in common, being from another, though not as to their proper character.
claims: Mission includes the common notion of being from another.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3529.summary: Reply to the second argument. Mission involves not only the effect of a created gift conferred on the creature but also the authority of a principle over the one sent, so in a person's mission the person is known to be from another. Since this does not fit the whole Trinity or the Father, they cannot be said to be sent. Also, that effect is appropriated more to one person than another, by which one person is said to be sent and not the other.
claims: Mission manifests a person as from another, which excludes the Father and the Trinity as a whole.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3533.summary: Reply to the third argument. Power, appropriated to the Father, does not pertain to the return to the end but rather to the going out from the principle, since power has the character of a principle. So it does not pertain to mission, which is for calling the rational creature back to God. Also the Father, in whom is first authority, cannot be said to be sent, since no one has authority over him.
claims: Power pertains to the going out of creatures, not to their return, and so not to mission.
The Father, having first authority, cannot be sent.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3536.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Since the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and both in the Spirit, when the Son is sent the Father and the Spirit also come, whether in the Son's coming in the flesh ('I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me', John 8:16) or in his coming into the mind ('we will come to him and make our abode with him', John 14:23). So coming and indwelling belong to the whole Trinity, being said only by reason of an effect that joins one to the Trinity, though by appropriation that effect may lead more to one person. Mission adds the authority of someone over the person sent and so can belong only to a person from another principle.
claims: Coming and indwelling belong to the whole Trinity; mission adds authority and so belongs only to Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3545.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Although knowledge is appropriated to the Son, the gift from which the experiential knowledge required for mission is taken is not necessarily appropriated to the Son; sometimes it is appropriated to the Spirit, as love.
claims: The experiential knowledge in mission can come through love, appropriated to the Spirit.

ta-l1d15q2-d1e3548.summary: Reply to the sixth argument. In a gift two things can be considered: the character of gift, by which every gift manifests the Spirit as first gift, since he is love; and the species of the gift, by which some gifts manifest the Son, like wisdom or knowledge.
claims: Every gift as gift manifests the Spirit; some gifts by their species manifest the Son.

ta-l1d15q2-Dd1e3493.summary: Article 1 (the only article) asks to whom it belongs to be sent. Against arguments for the whole Trinity, the Son alone, or the Spirit alone, Thomas holds that mission implies authority of a sender over the one sent, and among divine persons authority exists only by origin. So only Son and Spirit, who are from another, are sent, not the Father or the Trinity. Coming and indwelling belong to the whole Trinity, but mission adds authority. Power, appropriated to the Father, concerns going out rather than return. The gifts of mission manifest the Spirit as first gift and the Son by their species, such as wisdom.
claims: Only the Son and the Holy Spirit are sent; the Father is never sent.
Indwelling belongs to the whole Trinity; mission adds authority of origin.

ta-l1d15q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 15 asks to whom mission belongs. Because mission implies authority of a sender, and authority among divine persons exists only by origin, only the Son and the Spirit, who are from another, can be sent. The Father and the Trinity as a whole cannot. The whole Trinity comes and dwells in the soul, but mission adds the relation of origin. The gifts of mission manifest the Spirit as first gift and the Son through gifts of wisdom and knowledge, while power, appropriated to the Father, pertains to creatures' going out rather than to their return.
claims: Only the Son and the Holy Spirit can be sent, since mission implies authority of origin.
The whole Trinity indwells, but only the proceeding persons are sent.
